playbooks.title: Command and control channel
playbooks.summary: A host keeps calling the same outside address on a regular or opaque channel. Decide whether it is software phoning home or something you must contain.

steps.question: Is the timing machine-regular, and does it run all day?
steps.why: Malware beacons on a timer with little jitter and keeps going overnight. People and most update agents do not.
steps.normal: Bursty, human-paced contacts, or a known updater's schedule.
steps.bad: A steady interval with low jitter that continues through idle hours.

pivots.label: Every connection between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, pkts, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c, sni, ja4 FROM flow WHERE (src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_ip = '{peer}') OR (src_ip = '{peer}' AND dst_ip = '{actor}') ORDER BY start_ts

pivots.label: Packets between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer}

steps.question: Is the peer already known bad?
steps.why: An intel or reputation hit turns a suspicion into a confirmed lead, and decides how fast you contain.
steps.normal: No feed hit and a clean or unknown reputation.
steps.bad: Any IOC feed hit, or several engines calling it malicious.

steps.question: Is this new to the network?
steps.why: Malware infrastructure is almost always new to an environment. Something every host has used for months rarely is.
steps.normal: The peer, domain or client software appears in earlier captures.
steps.bad: First seen in this capture, or only this host uses it.

steps.question: What name does the peer go by?
steps.why: A legitimate service has a name that fits it. Bare IPs, missing SNI and freshly registered or random-looking domains do not.
steps.normal: A well-known vendor domain that matches the certificate.
steps.bad: No name at all, a random-looking name, or a mismatch with the certificate.

pivots.label: Flows naming {domain}
pivots.value: {domain}

pivots.label: Every flow that named {domain}
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, src_ip, dst_ip, dst_port, sni, http_host FROM flow WHERE sni LIKE '%{domain}' OR http_host LIKE '%{domain}' ORDER BY start_ts

steps.question: Does any other host talk to {peer}?
steps.why: One host means a single infection or a single odd app. Several hosts with the same pattern means wider compromise or a shared tool.
steps.normal: Many hosts, consistent with a shared corporate service.
steps.bad: A small set of hosts with the same timing and client software.

pivots.label: Hosts that contacted {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out, MIN(start_ts) AS first_seen FROM flow WHERE dst_ip = '{peer}' GROUP BY src_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

pivots.label: All flows to {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: Which client software made the connection?
steps.why: The JA4 or User-Agent points at the process. An unusual fingerprint on one host is a strong lead.
steps.normal: A browser or agent fingerprint the rest of the fleet shares.
steps.bad: A fingerprint only this host has, or a scripting runtime.

pivots.label: Client fingerprints and user agents on {actor}
pivots.value: SELECT ja4, ja3, http_ua, COUNT(*) AS flows FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' GROUP BY ja4, ja3, http_ua ORDER BY flows DESC

steps.question: What did {actor} do next?
steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: DNS tunneling or DGA
playbooks.summary: A host is sending unusual DNS: long random labels, high volume to one zone, or many random domains. Work out whether it is a tunnel, malware hunting for its C2, or a noisy product.

steps.question: Which zone carries the traffic?
steps.why: Tunnels and DGAs concentrate on one parent domain or a family of random ones. Security products and CDNs also use long labels, so the zone tells them apart.
steps.normal: A known vendor zone such as an antivirus or CDN lookup service.
steps.bad: An unfamiliar or newly seen zone, or many unregistered random names.

pivots.label: Flows naming {domain}
pivots.value: {domain}

pivots.label: Every flow that named {domain}
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, src_ip, dst_ip, dst_port, sni, http_host FROM flow WHERE sni LIKE '%{domain}' OR http_host LIKE '%{domain}' ORDER BY start_ts

steps.question: Which resolver did it use?
steps.why: Hosts should use your internal resolvers. Direct queries to an outside resolver bypass your DNS logging.
steps.normal: The corporate resolvers.
steps.bad: A public resolver queried directly, or DNS over HTTPS hiding the rest.

pivots.label: Where {actor} sent DNS
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_port IN (53, 853) GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port ORDER BY flows DESC

pivots.label: DNS packets from {actor}
pivots.value: host {actor} and port 53

steps.question: How much data moved through DNS?
steps.why: A tunnel moves real data, so the bytes per query and the total stand out next to normal lookups.
steps.normal: A handful of small queries.
steps.bad: Thousands of queries, or kilobytes of query names in a short time.

pivots.label: {actor}'s DNS traffic during the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, pkts, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_port = 53 AND start_ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '{start}' AND TIMESTAMP '{end}' ORDER BY start_ts

steps.question: Is the domain or its resolver already known bad?
steps.why: An intel or reputation hit turns a suspicion into a confirmed lead, and decides how fast you contain.
steps.normal: No feed hit and a clean or unknown reputation.
steps.bad: Any IOC feed hit, or several engines calling it malicious.

steps.question: Which machine is {actor}, and who uses it?
steps.why: Containment and the business impact depend on what the box is: a server, a workstation, a printer, a jump host.
steps.normal: A known asset whose role matches this traffic.
steps.bad: An unknown MAC, an unexpected vendor, or a role that should never do this.

steps.question: What did {actor} do next?
steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: ICMP tunnel
playbooks.summary: A host keeps a large-payload ICMP echo channel open. Pings are tiny; a sustained data channel over ICMP is a covert path.

steps.question: Do the echo payloads carry data?
steps.why: Normal ping payloads are small and repetitive. Tunnels carry variable, high-entropy payloads.
steps.normal: Fixed small payloads from a monitoring tool.
steps.bad: Large or changing payloads, in both directions.

pivots.label: ICMP packets between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer} and icmp

steps.question: Is {actor} a monitoring system?
steps.why: Network monitors ping constantly and are the usual benign explanation.
steps.normal: A known monitoring host pinging many devices.
steps.bad: A workstation pinging one outside address.

steps.question: Is the peer already known bad?
steps.why: An intel or reputation hit turns a suspicion into a confirmed lead, and decides how fast you contain.
steps.normal: No feed hit and a clean or unknown reputation.
steps.bad: Any IOC feed hit, or several engines calling it malicious.

steps.normal: The peer, domain or client software appears in earlier captures.
steps.bad: First seen in this capture, or only this host uses it.

steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: Data exfiltration
playbooks.summary: A host sent far more out than it received to one peer. Decide what left, where it went, and whether it was sanctioned.

steps.question: Where did the data go?
steps.why: Sanctioned uploads go to known storage and backup services. Exfiltration often lands on fresh infrastructure or personal storage.
steps.normal: Corporate cloud storage or a backup provider.
steps.bad: A new, unnamed or personal storage destination.

pivots.label: All flows to {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: How much left, and over how long?
steps.why: The size and pacing tell you whether this was a bulk grab or a slow drip.
steps.normal: A size and schedule that match a known job.
steps.bad: Gigabytes at an odd hour, or a long low-rate stream.

pivots.label: Every connection between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, pkts, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c, sni, ja4 FROM flow WHERE (src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_ip = '{peer}') OR (src_ip = '{peer}' AND dst_ip = '{actor}') ORDER BY start_ts

pivots.label: {actor}'s biggest outbound destinations
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY bytes_out DESC

steps.question: What happened before the upload?
steps.why: Exfiltration usually follows collection: internal file-share reads, archive downloads, or database pulls.
steps.normal: No unusual internal reads before.
steps.bad: Heavy reads from file shares or databases shortly before.

pivots.label: {actor}'s traffic during the alert window
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c, sni, http_host FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '{start}' AND TIMESTAMP '{end}' ORDER BY start_ts

steps.question: Is the peer already known bad?
steps.why: An intel or reputation hit turns a suspicion into a confirmed lead, and decides how fast you contain.
steps.normal: No feed hit and a clean or unknown reputation.
steps.bad: Any IOC feed hit, or several engines calling it malicious.

steps.question: Which machine is {actor}, and who uses it?
steps.why: Containment and the business impact depend on what the box is: a server, a workstation, a printer, a jump host.
steps.normal: A known asset whose role matches this traffic.
steps.bad: An unknown MAC, an unexpected vendor, or a role that should never do this.

playbooks.title: Scan or sweep
playbooks.summary: One host probed many hosts or many ports. Find out whether it is an authorized scanner, and if not, what it found.

steps.question: Is {actor} an authorized scanner?
steps.why: Vulnerability scanners and monitoring tools explain most scans. Check your scanner list before anything else.
steps.normal: A documented scanner running on its usual schedule.
steps.bad: A workstation or server with no scanning role.

steps.question: Which targets answered?
steps.why: A scan matters most where it found an open service. Those hosts are the next targets.
steps.normal: Few or no responses.
steps.bad: Open admin services (SMB, RDP, SSH, WinRM) on many hosts.

pivots.label: Targets that sent data back to {actor}
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_s2c) AS bytes_back FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_ip IN ({victims}) GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY dst_ip

pivots.label: Where {actor} connected and got data back
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND bytes_s2c > 0 GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY flows DESC

steps.question: Did the scan come from outside, or after an inbound connection?
steps.why: An internal host that starts scanning right after an unusual inbound session or download is likely compromised.
steps.normal: No unusual inbound traffic before the scan.
steps.bad: A new inbound session or download just before the scan began.

pivots.label: Who connected to {actor}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, MIN(start_ts) AS first_seen FROM flow WHERE dst_ip = '{actor}' GROUP BY src_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY first_seen

steps.question: What did {actor} do next?
steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: Brute force or password spray
playbooks.summary: Many authentication attempts against one service or many accounts. Decide whether any attempt worked.

steps.question: Did any attempt succeed?
steps.why: A failed spray is noise. One success is a compromised account.
steps.normal: Only failures, then the source stops.
steps.bad: A long session or data transfer after the attempts.

pivots.label: Every connection between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, pkts, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c, sni, ja4 FROM flow WHERE (src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_ip = '{peer}') OR (src_ip = '{peer}' AND dst_ip = '{actor}') ORDER BY start_ts

pivots.label: Packets between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer} and port {port}

steps.question: How many services or hosts were targeted?
steps.why: One target suggests a misconfigured client. Many targets suggest an attacker.
steps.normal: One service and a stuck password.
steps.bad: Several hosts on the same port.

pivots.label: Every source hitting port {port}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE dst_port = {port} GROUP BY src_ip, dst_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

steps.question: Is the source internal, and should it authenticate here?
steps.why: An internal workstation spraying a domain controller is a compromised host. An internet source is exposure.
steps.normal: A service account with a known expired password.
steps.bad: A workstation or an outside address.

steps.question: What did {actor} do next?
steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: Cleartext credentials or personal data
playbooks.summary: Credentials or personal data crossed the network unencrypted. Scope what was exposed and who could see it.

steps.question: Which credentials or data were exposed?
steps.why: Rotation and notification depend on exactly what was sent.
steps.normal: Test accounts or synthetic data.
steps.bad: Real user, admin or service credentials, or customer data.

pivots.label: Packets between {actor} and {peer}
pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer} and port {port}

steps.question: Did the traffic leave the network?
steps.why: Cleartext inside a segment is a hygiene problem. Cleartext over the internet means the data must be treated as disclosed.
steps.normal: Internal segment only.
steps.bad: The peer is outside the network.

pivots.label: All flows to {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: Were the exposed credentials used anywhere else?
steps.why: An attacker sniffing the wire will try the same credentials on other services.
steps.normal: No other logins from unusual hosts.
steps.bad: The same service seen from new hosts after the exposure.

pivots.label: Every source hitting port {port}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE dst_port = {port} GROUP BY src_ip, dst_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

playbooks.title: Lateral movement or remote execution
playbooks.summary: A host opened admin sessions to other internal hosts, or created a service or task on one. Decide whether it is IT administration or an attacker spreading.

steps.question: Is {actor} an admin or management host?
steps.why: Jump hosts, deployment servers and IT workstations do this every day. User workstations should not.
steps.normal: A documented management system during a change window.
steps.bad: A user workstation, or a server that never administers others.

steps.question: Which hosts did it reach, and how?
steps.why: The protocol and target list show the technique (SMB service creation, WinRM, RDP) and where to look next.
steps.normal: A small set of expected servers.
steps.bad: Many workstations, or domain controllers and file servers.

pivots.label: Sessions from {actor} to its targets
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_s2c) AS bytes_back FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND dst_ip IN ({victims}) GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY dst_ip

pivots.label: {actor}'s internal destinations
pivots.value: SELECT dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' GROUP BY dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY bytes_out DESC

steps.question: How did {actor} get compromised?
steps.why: The host doing the spreading was itself entered somehow. Its own inbound connections and downloads show how.
steps.normal: Nothing unusual reached it first.
steps.bad: An inbound session, phishing download or beacon before the spread.

pivots.label: Who connected to {actor}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, dst_port, app_proto, COUNT(*) AS flows, MIN(start_ts) AS first_seen FROM flow WHERE dst_ip = '{actor}' GROUP BY src_ip, dst_port, app_proto ORDER BY first_seen

steps.question: What did {actor} do next?
steps.why: Attackers rarely stop at one step. The traffic right after the detection shows whether it worked.
steps.normal: Ordinary traffic resumes.
steps.bad: New internal connections, downloads, credential traffic or uploads soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

playbooks.title: Signature rule match
playbooks.summary: An imported signature fired. Check the rule against the traffic before trusting it.

steps.question: What does the rule look for, and is it reliable?
steps.why: Community rules range from precise to very broad. Read the rule and its references first.
steps.normal: A broad policy or informational rule.
steps.bad: A specific rule for a named malware family or exploit.

pivots.label: All flows to {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: Does the payload actually match the threat?
steps.why: Signatures fire on fragments. The packets show whether the content really is the attack.
steps.normal: The match is in benign content, such as a documentation page.
steps.bad: The full exploit or malware traffic is visible.

pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer} and port {port}

playbooks.title: TLS, SSH or certificate posture
playbooks.summary: A server offered weak protocol settings or a bad certificate. Usually a hardening task, sometimes interception.

steps.question: Which server is it, and who owns it?
steps.why: Posture issues are fixed by the server owner, so identify the service first.
steps.normal: A known internal appliance with an owner.
steps.bad: An unknown server, or an outside service your users depend on.

pivots.label: All flows to {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: Could this be interception rather than old configuration?
steps.why: A self-signed or mismatched certificate on a well-known site is how a man-in-the-middle looks.
steps.normal: The same certificate across captures for an internal service.
steps.bad: A new self-signed certificate on a public name.

pivots.label: Hosts that contacted {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out, MIN(start_ts) AS first_seen FROM flow WHERE dst_ip = '{peer}' GROUP BY src_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

steps.question: Which clients still negotiate the weak setting?
steps.why: Disabling the weak option breaks these clients, so list them before remediation.
steps.normal: No clients, or only legacy test systems.
steps.bad: Production clients that need upgrading first.

pivots.label: Hosts that contacted {peer}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out, MIN(start_ts) AS first_seen FROM flow WHERE dst_ip = '{peer}' GROUP BY src_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

playbooks.title: ARP spoofing
playbooks.summary: One IP address was claimed by more than one MAC. That is either a failover pair or someone positioning to intercept traffic.

steps.question: Which MACs claimed the address, and which is legitimate?
steps.why: The vendor and switch port of each MAC tell you which device is the impostor.
steps.normal: A documented HA pair or a VM migration.
steps.bad: An unknown MAC claiming the gateway or a server.

pivots.value: arp and host {actor}

steps.question: Is the claimed address the gateway or a key server?
steps.why: Spoofing the gateway intercepts a whole segment.
steps.normal: An ordinary host address.
steps.bad: The default gateway, DNS or a domain controller.

pivots.label: All flows touching {actor}
pivots.value: {actor}

steps.question: How many sources are there?
steps.why: One source is easy to block. Thousands of spoofed sources need upstream help.
steps.normal: One misbehaving client.
steps.bad: Many sources, or spoofed random addresses.

pivots.label: Every source hitting port {port}
pivots.value: SELECT src_ip, dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS flows, SUM(bytes_c2s) AS bytes_out FROM flow WHERE dst_port = {port} GROUP BY src_ip, dst_ip ORDER BY flows DESC

steps.question: Did legitimate clients still complete connections?
steps.why: Impact decides urgency.

playbooks.summary: A known attack or scanning tool identified itself. Confirm whether it is authorized testing.

steps.question: Is there an authorized test running from {actor}?
steps.why: Penetration tests and red teams use these tools. Check with whoever owns testing.

steps.bad: No test on record, or an unexpected source.

steps.question: What did the tool hit, and did it get answers?
steps.why: Successful responses (200s, logins, data) show what the tool reached.
steps.normal: Errors and blocks only.
steps.bad: Successful responses from sensitive applications.

pivots.value: host {actor} and host {peer}

playbooks.title: Malware delivery
playbooks.summary: A host downloaded a file that is malware or pretends to be something else. Treat the host as infected until shown otherwise.

steps.question: What is the file, and is it known?
steps.why: The hash is the fastest way to a verdict and the key to hunting the same file elsewhere.
steps.normal: An installer from a vendor whose content type was simply mislabeled.
steps.bad: A known-bad hash, a signature hit, or an executable posing as an image.

pivots.label: Flows to the download server {peer}
pivots.value: {peer}

steps.question: Did it run?
steps.why: Delivery is not infection. Traffic after the download shows whether the payload executed.
steps.normal: Nothing new after the download.
steps.bad: New beacons, DNS or downloads from {actor} soon after.

pivots.label: Everything {actor} opened from the start of the alert
pivots.value: SELECT start_ts, dst_ip, dst_port, app_proto, bytes_c2s, bytes_s2c FROM flow WHERE src_ip = '{actor}' AND start_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{start}' ORDER BY start_ts

steps.question: Did anyone else download it?
steps.why: The same file or server on other hosts widens the incident.
steps.normal: Only this host.
steps.bad: Several hosts fetched it.

steps.question: Which pool, and since when?

steps.normal: A sanctioned research or lab system.

playbooks.title: Exposed remote access
playbooks.summary: A remote administration session crossed the network boundary. Find out whether that path is meant to exist.

steps.question: Who started it, and from where?
steps.why: Inbound sessions from the internet to RDP, SMB or SSH are a top initial access route.
steps.normal: An outbound session to a known vendor support portal.
steps.bad: Inbound from an unknown internet address.

playbooks.title: Industrial control command
playbooks.summary: A client wrote to or controlled an industrial device. Verify it was an authorized operator action.

steps.question: Is {actor} an authorized HMI or engineering workstation?
steps.why: Only a short list of hosts should ever write to PLCs.
steps.normal: The plant's HMI during a shift.
steps.bad: Any other host, or an IT network address.

steps.question: Which commands were sent, and to what?
steps.why: Writes to setpoints or stop commands can have physical consequences.
steps.normal: Routine reads and expected setpoint changes.
steps.bad: Writes to safety-related registers, or many devices at once.

steps.question: How did {actor} reach the control network?

playbooks.title: Change from normal behavior
playbooks.summary: A host did something it never did before, or its traffic broke from its own trend. Decide whether it is planned change or compromise.

steps.question: What exactly is new for {actor}?
steps.why: The specific new peer, port or volume is what you will check against change records.
steps.normal: A new update server or a new application rollout.
steps.bad: A new outside peer with no business reason.

steps.question: Was there planned change at that time?

steps.normal: A matching change ticket or maintenance window.

steps.question: Did new software appear on {actor}?
steps.why: New client software alongside new destinations is the classic sign of an implant.

playbooks.summary: The protocol does not match the port: TLS on a port no service uses, or something other than TLS on 443. Usually misconfiguration, sometimes evasion.

steps.question: What service is really there?
steps.why: Naming the real service tells you whether this is a sanctioned app.
steps.normal: A known application on a custom port.
steps.bad: An unidentified service, or a tunnel on 443.

playbooks.title: Kerberoasting or AS-REP roasting
playbooks.summary: A host pulled Kerberos tickets in a form that can be cracked offline. Assume the targeted service account passwords are at risk.

steps.question: Which accounts were targeted?
steps.why: Rotation starts with the roasted accounts, and privileged ones come first.
steps.normal: A single service account requested by its usual client.
steps.bad: Many SPNs, or accounts with admin rights.

steps.question: Is {actor} a normal Kerberos client for those services?
steps.why: Workstations that suddenly request tickets for many services are running a tool.
steps.normal: An application server that always uses these services.
steps.bad: A user workstation requesting dozens of tickets at once.

steps.question: Did directory reconnaissance come first?
steps.why: Roasting usually follows LDAP queries for SPN holders.
steps.normal: No LDAP searches before.
steps.bad: LDAP or SAMR enumeration shortly before.

playbooks.title: DCSync
playbooks.summary: A host that is not a domain controller asked a DC to replicate secrets. Unless it is a real DC or a sanctioned sync tool, assume domain credentials are stolen.

steps.question: Is {actor} a domain controller or an approved sync tool?
steps.why: Only DCs and a few identity products replicate. Everything else is credential theft.
steps.normal: A new DC being promoted, or Azure AD Connect.
steps.bad: A workstation or member server.

steps.question: How did the attacker get replication rights?
steps.why: DCSync needs domain admin-level rights, so the account used is already compromised.
steps.bad: Admin sessions to {actor} shortly before.
